notes: Renewed permission appeal on conditional leave to defend in fraud claim; refusal to vary payment-in condition upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Berezovsky v Wah: conditional leave to defend after freezing order breach
key_facts: The claimants alleged the defendant fraudulently induced them to part with $5 million by deceit and constructive trust claims.
The defendant breached a freezing order and failed to comply with disclosure obligations.
Gray J refused to debar the defendant from defending but ordered payment into court of $2.5 million as a condition of defending.
The defendant sought to reduce the condition to $1.2 million on the ground it was stifling but never paid even that sum into court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against orders requiring payment into court as a condition of defending.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the Court of Appeal upheld Gray J's refusal to vary the $2.5 million payment-in condition.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant seeks to vary a conditional leave to defend order on the ground that the sum required is stifling, he must prove that with full chapter and verse; a bare assertion on oath is insufficient, especially where disclosure has been deficient and the defence is shadowy.
legal_issues: Whether the payment-in condition was stifling
Whether Gray J erred in refusing to reduce the condition from $2.5 million to $1.2 million
Whether conditional leave to defend was appropriate after flagrant breach of a freezing order

confidence.notes: Short procedural judgment with clear outcome and reasoning on the stifling issue.

notes: Local councillor code-of-conduct appeal; objective test for personal and prejudicial interests affirmed.

enrichment.short_title: Scrivens v ESO: objective test for councillor prejudicial interests
key_facts: Councillor Victor Scrivens was suspended for four months by an Adjudication Panel case tribunal for breaches of Farnham Town Council's code of conduct.
The tribunal found failures to declare prejudicial and personal interests in relation to theatre funding, church grants and a plans panel matter.
Scrivens argued a councillor does not breach the code if he honestly and reasonably but mistakenly believes he has no relevant interest.
The tribunal applied an objective test; Scrivens appealed under section 79(15) of the 2000 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 79(15) of the Local Government Act 2000 against Adjudication Panel findings of code breaches.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; whether a member has a personal or prejudicial interest and whether he failed to comply with the code are determined objectively.
enrichment.ratio: Personal and prejudicial interests under the parish council model code are questions to be determined objectively; a member's honest but mistaken belief that he has no such interest does not prevent a finding of failure to comply with paragraphs 8 and 10, and paragraph 76 of Richardson was obiter on the subjective test.
legal_issues: Whether the test for personal and prejudicial interests is subjective (subject to rationality) or objective
Whether honest reasonable mistake excuses non-disclosure or failure to withdraw
Whether R (Richardson) v North Yorkshire County Council binds on the subjective test
linked_authorities: R (Richardson) v North Yorkshire County Council [2003] EWCA Civ 1860

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on a discrete statutory construction issue with clear final holdings.

notes: Interim injunction in business-sale restrictive covenant dispute; serious issue and balance of convenience found for claimant.

enrichment.short_title: Jewellery Appraisal Services v Belson: interim injunction on post-sale covenants
key_facts: The defendants sold a jewellery appraisal and insurer replacement business to the claimant in May 2003 under restrictive covenants lasting five years (later shortened).
The claimant alleged Mr Belson approached restricted insurer clients including Axa, Lloyds TSB and Direct Line and solicited staff.
In January 2005 Belson submitted a valuation report to Cunningham Lindsey stating it was submitted on behalf of Direct Line, a restricted client.
Belson contended he acted for the insured homeowner rather than the insurer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim application for injunction to restrain breach of restrictive covenants in a business sale agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted in principle; serious issue to be tried established on 2004 events and the Direct Line incident; balance of convenience favoured the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: At the interim stage the court may grant an injunction where there is a serious issue to be tried on covenant breach even based on disputed conversations and where the defendant's own email language supports the claimant's case; bare assertions alone are insufficient but corroborated evidence may suffice.
legal_issues: Whether there was a serious issue to be tried on alleged covenant breaches
Whether the Direct Line valuation work breached non-compete and non-solicitation covenants
Whether the balance of convenience favoured granting an injunction
linked_authorities: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396
Nottingham Building Society v Eurodynamics Systems Ltd [1993] FSR 468

confidence.notes: Interlocutory findings are explicit though final trial merits remain undetermined.

notes: Indecent assault conviction appeal dismissed; fresh chip-shop evidence held not capable of belief.

enrichment.short_title: R v Thackery: fresh evidence appeal after indecent assault conviction
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of indecently assaulting a 14-year-old girl, C, at her friend's home in September 2003; she did not complain until May 2004.
Fresh evidence related to an incident outside a chip shop shortly after conviction where appellant's supporters claimed C admitted making a false allegation.
C gave evidence that she only denied a rumour of rape and was threatened by supporters of the appellant.
Witness accounts from appellant's friends were inconsistent and C appeared genuinely distressed giving evidence again.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave on the ground of fresh evidence contradicting the complainant's trial evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the fresh evidence was not capable of belief.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh post-conviction evidence is incapable of belief where witness accounts are inconsistent, the complainant's crying is more likely explained by threatening behaviour than spontaneous remorse, and she consistently maintained she only denied a rape rumour rather than admitting a false assault allegation.
legal_issues: Whether fresh evidence contradicting the complainant is capable of belief
Whether C admitted fabricating the indecent assault allegation
Assessment of inconsistent accounts by appellant's supporters

confidence.notes: Credibility assessment is detailed though underlying trial facts are summarised only briefly.

notes: Brief GMC application extending interim suspension of convicted doctor; costs ordered against absent doctor.

enrichment.short_title: GMC v Sourial: extension of interim suspension after child cruelty conviction
key_facts: Dr Sourial was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment in January 2004 for child cruelty against her teenage niece and nephew.
Her GMC registration had been suspended since October 2002 and an earlier one-year extension was granted by consent in May 2004.
The GMC sought a further one-year extension of interim suspension expiring on 27 April 2005.
Dr Sourial did not attend the hearing despite repeated correspondence to her solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: GMC application to the High Court under section 41 of the Medical Act 1983 to extend interim suspension pending Professional Conduct Committee proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Interim suspension extended to 27 April 2006; Dr Sourial ordered to pay the costs of the hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where the statutory criteria in section 41 are satisfied the court may extend interim suspension; a doctor who fails to consent to a plainly appropriate extension and does not attend may be ordered to pay the costs unnecessarily incurred.
legal_issues: Whether interim suspension should be extended under section 41 of the Medical Act 1983
Whether Dr Sourial should bear the costs of the application

confidence.notes: Very short ex tempore-style order; legal basis and outcome are clear but detail is limited.

notes: Burglary convictions quashed; cell-refusal adverse inference direction held unlawful at common law.

enrichment.short_title: R v Johnson and Hind: section 34 and adverse inference from refusing interview

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Johnson and Hind were convicted of burglary and taking a Mercedes after a late-night break-in; fibre evidence linked them to the car.
Their defence was scavenging theft from an abandoned car rather than committing the burglary.
Hind positively refused to leave his cell for police interview; the judge directed the jury they could draw an adverse inference.
A juror was wrongly approached by a third party during trial but police found no link to the defendants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave on jury directions, section 34, identification and bad character points.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions quashed and retrial ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Section 34(1)(a) does not apply where no questions were put because the suspect refused to leave his cell; at common law preserved by section 34(5) the jury must not be invited to draw an adverse inference from refusal to be interviewed before trial, following Gilbert and Raviraj.
legal_issues: Whether section 34(1)(a) applies to refusal to leave a cell for interview
Whether adverse inference directions at common law were permissible
Whether jury directions on third-party juror approach were adequate
Whether Turnbull identification directions were deficient
linked_authorities: R v Gilbert (1978) 66 Cr App R 237
R v Raviraj (1987) 85 Cr App R 93
R v Webber [2004] 1 Cr App R 40

confidence.notes: Long appellate judgment with explicit holdings on section 34 and common law silence.

notes: MHRT judicial review on standard of proof; civil standard applies with careful hearsay approach.

enrichment.short_title: R (DJ and AN) v MHRT: standard of proof for discharge decisions
key_facts: Two restricted patients challenged Mental Health Review Tribunal refusals to discharge them under sections 72 and 73 of the 1983 Act.
AN's tribunal applied balance of probabilities for expert conflicts but a higher standard for important factual issues; DJ's tribunal used a similar approach.
MIND intervened arguing for criminal or clear-and-convincing standards and criticising reliance on hearsay conduct reports.
DJ had already been discharged by hospital managers before the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated judicial review applications challenging the standard of proof applied by the Mental Health Review Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Applications dismissed; the civil standard of proof applies where proof is relevant, with careful treatment of hearsay, and many criteria involve evaluative risk assessment rather than proof.
enrichment.ratio: Mental Health Review Tribunal discharge decisions under sections 72 and 73 generally require the civil standard where issues are susceptible to proof, not the criminal standard; tribunals must treat hearsay cautiously following Sim and Brooks, and many criteria involve forward-looking evaluative judgments rather than proof of past conduct.
legal_issues: Whether the criminal or civil standard of proof applies before the MHRT
Whether the concept of proof is relevant to all section 72 and 73 criteria
How tribunals should approach hearsay reports of patient conduct
linked_authorities: In re H (Minors) (Sexual Abuse: Standard of Proof) [1996] AC 563
R (Sim) v Parole Board [2003] EWCA Civ 1845
R (McCann) v Crown Court at Manchester [2002] UKHL 39

confidence.notes: Comprehensive judgment on standard of proof with clear dismissal of both claims.

notes: Costs judgment in long-running East Sussex community care litigation; 50% costs awarded for one period.

enrichment.short_title: R (A and B) v East Sussex: costs after manual handling JR litigation
key_facts: Disabled residents A and B and their carers X and Y challenged East Sussex County Council's care plans and manual handling policies in parallel judicial review and best interests proceedings from 2001.
Wilson J ordered ESCC to pay 85% of costs to June 2002; the best interests claim was largely abandoned as weak.
Munby J adjudicated legal issues on user independent trusts and manual handling principles but most factual disputes were never tried.
The proceedings concluded by consent in June 2004 with total claimant costs of about £750,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Written submissions on outstanding costs after consent orders resolving judicial review and best interests proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: ESCC ordered to pay 50% of both claimants' costs from 14 June 2002 to 25 November 2002; no order as to other periods; no order on the costs application itself.
enrichment.ratio: Where judicial review proceedings settle without full adjudication of substantive factual issues, costs may be apportioned under Boxall principles; success on discrete legal issues such as user independent trusts and manual handling law can justify partial recovery even where vast expert evidence on untried facts cannot be fully rewarded.
legal_issues: Apportionment of costs where proceedings settled without trial of substantive facts
Whether two sets of claimant costs should be allowed
Application of Boxall where no final determination on the claim
Costs of best interests proceedings
linked_authorities: R (Boxall) v Waltham Forest LBC (2000) 4 CCLR 258
R (A, B, X and Y) v East Sussex County Council (No 2) [2003] EWHC 167 (Admin)
R (Cowl) v Plymouth City Council [2001] EWCA Civ 1935

confidence.notes: Costs-only judgment; substantive merits largely settled elsewhere but cost apportionment reasoning is clear.

notes: Reinsurance forum conveniens appeal dismissed; Dispute Clause confined to North American claims.

enrichment.short_title: Limit v PDVIC: forum conveniens for Venezuelan oil pollution retrocession
key_facts: PDVSA suffered pollution losses from 1998 and 2001 pipeline leaks in Venezuela and sought cover under policies reinsured through London market retrocessionaires Limit.
Limit issued English proceedings for declarations of non-liability before any Venezuelan claim was brought.
Retrocession slips contained a Dispute Clause attached separately; Moore-Bick J held it applied only to North American claims.
Most evidence, landowners and underlying insurance issues were connected with Venezuela.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against setting aside permission to serve out of the jurisdiction and declining English forum for declaratory relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Dispute Clause was confined to USA/Canadian claims and Venezuela was the forum conveniens.
enrichment.ratio: A Dispute Clause physically attached to a London market retrocession slip but referenced only in the USA/Canadian jurisdiction section applies to that special regime only; where Venezuelan pipeline losses are in issue and underlying disputes remain untried there, England is not clearly the appropriate forum for premature retrocession declarations.
legal_issues: Construction of the Dispute Clause in 1997 and 1999 retrocession slips
Whether English or Venezuelan courts are forum conveniens
Appropriateness of declaratory proceedings before underlying claims are issued
linked_authorities: Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460
HIH Casualty & General Insurance Ltd v New Hampshire Insurance Co [2001] LLR IR 224

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate judgment on jurisdiction clause construction and Spiliada discretion.

notes: Halkyn Mountain candidate SAC challenge dismissed on consultation and substantive grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Newsum v Welsh Assembly: challenge to Halkyn Mountain candidate SAC
key_facts: The Duke of Westminster's trustees own most of Halkyn Mountain in North East Wales, designated a Special Area of Conservation for calaminarian grassland and great crested newts.
They challenged the Welsh Assembly Government's March 2003 decision to include the site on the candidate SAC list submitted to the European Commission.
The claim alleged inadequate consultation and irrational inclusion of quarry, grassland and golf course areas.
The defendant argued the claim was pointless after final SAC designation and out of time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Rolled-up judicial review of the decision to include Halkyn Mountain as a candidate Special Area of Conservation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but claim dismissed; challenge failed on consultation and all substantive grounds.
enrichment.ratio: A candidate SAC listing decision may be defended where consultation followed the scientific selection process and inclusion of an open space under a single management regime rather than tightly demarcating habitat patches is not irrational; final SAC designation does not necessarily deprive a candidate listing challenge of all purpose where permission is argued.
legal_issues: Whether proceedings challenging candidate SAC listing remained useful after final designation
Whether consultation on scientific rationale was adequate
Rationality of including Pen yr Henblas Quarry, calaminarian grassland areas and Holywell Golf Course

confidence.notes: Full rolled-up hearing with detailed habitat and consultation analysis and clear dismissal.
